hydroquinone.summary: Prescription skin lightener that fades dark spots, melasma and acne marks for a more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Hydroquinone is a topical skin lightener used to fade melasma, sun spots and post-acne marks, giving a more even complexion. It has been used for decades and is often described as the reference treatment for stubborn pigment.

It works by blocking tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and by disrupting pigment-cell activity, so existing dark patches lighten as new pigment slows. A 2022 systematic review calls it the gold standard in melasma, and a 2020 review found it, alone or in a triple combination cream with tretinoin and a corticosteroid, among the most effective melasma treatments examined.
quick.how: People use it as a prescription or compounded cream applied to the affected patches, usually in supervised courses rather than continuously, and paired with daily sunscreen so spots do not return. It is often combined with a retinoid or other lightening agents. Results build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Irritation and contact dermatitis are the common effects. Long-term or high-strength use, especially of unregulated products, can cause exogenous ochronosis, a hard-to-treat blue-black discoloration, and paradoxical darkening. Regulation varies: cosmetic use is restricted or banned in the EU, Japan and Australia, and the US FDA withdrew over-the-counter hydroquinone in 2020 while prescription products remain available.

angle.text: Hydroquinone is used to fade melasma, sun spots and post-acne marks for a more even skin tone. It blocks pigment production so dark patches lighten over weeks. Clinical studies document the lightening effect; forum discussion focuses on safety limits and the risk of paradoxical darkening with long, high-strength use.

alpha-arbutin.summary: Over-the-counter serum ingredient that gently fades dark spots and acne marks for a more even tone.

quick.overview:
Alpha-arbutin is a serum ingredient used to fade dark spots, acne marks, freckles and uneven tone. It is marketed as a gentler alternative to hydroquinone and sold without a prescription.

It competitively inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin production, and releases slowly in the skin, which is thought to make it milder. Lab studies show reduced melanin in cultured cells and a 3D skin model without loss of cell viability. Human trials are mostly small, and many test combination products rather than alpha-arbutin alone.
quick.how: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, usually daily alongside sunscreen, and layered with other brightening or exfoliating actives. Fading is gradual, typically over several weeks to a couple of months.
quick.risks: Side effects are generally mild, mainly occasional irritation. Because it can release small amounts of hydroquinone, the EU's consumer safety committee has set limits of 2 percent in face creams and 0.5 percent in body lotions. Reported results are modest compared with prescription treatments.

angle.text: Alpha-arbutin is a serum ingredient people use to fade dark spots, acne marks and uneven tone. It slows the enzyme that makes pigment, so spots lighten gradually without the strength of hydroquinone. Small studies have measured lightening; under-eye darkness has been studied less.

kojic-acid.summary: Fungal-derived brightening ingredient in creams and soaps that lightens dark spots and melasma.

quick.overview:
Kojic acid is a compound made by Aspergillus fungi, including in rice fermented for sake, and is used in brightening creams, serums and soaps to lighten dark spots, acne marks and melasma.

It binds copper at the active site of tyrosinase, blocking the enzyme that begins melanin production, and it has antioxidant activity. Reviews list it among conventional first-line topical agents for hyperpigmentation. In a 60-patient Indian study, 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than a 0.75 percent kojic acid cream that also contained vitamin C, and other trials test it inside combination products.
quick.how: People use it as a cream, serum or soap, often as part of a brightening routine with sunscreen and other pigment-fading ingredients. Results typically build over weeks to months. It is sensitive to light and air, so packaging matters.
quick.risks: Contact dermatitis and irritation are the main concerns. In the EU a 2024 regulation allows it only in face and hand products at up to 1 percent, applying to products placed on the market from 1 November 2025. Long-term safety data are limited, and it does not replace sun protection.

angle.text: Kojic acid is used in brightening creams and soaps to lighten dark spots, acne marks and melasma. It blocks the pigment-making enzyme, so patches fade gradually. Small studies have looked at melasma; irritation is commonly reported, and under-eye use has been studied less.

cysteamine.summary: Topical cream that lightens melasma and dark spots as a non-hydroquinone option for more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Cysteamine cream is used to lighten melasma and dark spots and is discussed as a non-hydroquinone alternative. Its main medical use is a rare metabolic disease, nephropathic cystinosis.

In skin it is thought to inhibit tyrosinase and peroxidase, scavenge free radicals and bind iron and copper, which reduces melanin formation. Controlled studies in melasma have shown improvement over vehicle, and a 2025 double-blind trial compared an overnight cream containing 5 percent cysteamine and ectoine with 4 percent hydroquinone cream.
quick.how: People use it as a leave-on cream, sometimes overnight or as a short-contact application, over a course of weeks, with daily sunscreen. It is often chosen by those who want to avoid hydroquinone. Lightening takes time, as with most pigment treatments.
quick.risks: The main drawbacks are a strong sulfurous odor, stinging and redness, and instability, since the molecule oxidizes in air. Systemic cysteamine drugs have gastrointestinal and other side effects, and whether it is sold as a cosmetic or a medicine varies by country.

angle.text: Cysteamine cream is used to lighten melasma patches and dark spots, often as an alternative to hydroquinone. It suppresses melanin production so pigment fades over weeks. Several small to moderate melasma trials exist, while use on otherwise healthy skin has been studied less.

salicylic-acid.summary: Oil-soluble BHA that clears pores, blackheads and body acne for clearer, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid used in washes, toners and spot treatments to clear blackheads, oily skin and acne on the face, back and chest. It also helps prevent ingrown hairs after shaving and is used for dandruff, warts and keratosis pilaris.

Because it dissolves in oil, it works inside pores, loosening the bonds between dead skin cells and dissolving lipids in clogged follicles, with mild anti-inflammatory effects. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for topical salicylic acid.
quick.how: People use it as a daily or every-other-day wash, leave-on liquid or pad, often alongside benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, and with moisturizer and sunscreen. Fewer clogged pores usually show over several weeks. Body washes are common for chest and back acne.
quick.risks: Dryness, peeling, burning and irritation are common with stronger products. Salicylate absorption and toxicity have been documented with very large-area, high-strength use, so caution applies in children, in pregnancy and on broken skin. Photosensitivity is mild, and sunscreen is advised.

angle.text: Salicylic acid washes and leave-ons are used for blackheads, body acne and ingrown hairs after shaving. It dissolves oil and dead skin inside pores, so fewer pores clog and skin looks clearer. It is a standard acne ingredient; users report dryness and burning with strong products.

glycolic-acid.summary: AHA exfoliant that sheds dull surface cells for brighter, smoother skin and fewer fine lines.

quick.overview:
Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid and one of the most widely used chemical exfoliants. People use it for dullness, rough texture, dark spots, acne marks and fine lines, in home products and professional peels.

It weakens the bonds between surface skin cells so dull cells shed faster, and with repeated use it stimulates epidermal renewal and has been reported to increase dermal collagen. Trials show modest improvements in texture and photoaging, and a 2024 systematic review of chemical peels for melasma (24 studies, 1,075 participants) concluded glycolic acid was the most safe and effective peeling agent among those studied.
quick.how: At home it comes as toners, serums and pads used a few nights a week, with sunscreen by day. Stronger peels are done in clinics. Users often debate strength and frequency, and glow and texture changes show up over weeks of regular use.
quick.risks: Stinging, redness and peeling are common, and skin becomes more sensitive to sunlight, so sunscreen is advised. Excess strength or poor technique can cause burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin tones. Peel depth is linked to both results and complications.

angle.text: Glycolic acid is used as an exfoliant for dullness, rough texture, dark spots, acne marks and fine lines. It loosens dead surface skin so cells shed faster and skin looks smoother and brighter. Trials show modest texture and photoaging gains; stronger products commonly irritate.

lactic-acid.summary: Milder AHA that exfoliates and hydrates for softer, brighter, smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Lactic acid is an alpha hydroxy acid used in serums, peels and body lotions to smooth texture, brighten dullness, even tone and soften dry, rough skin. It is often chosen by people with sensitive skin because it is typically milder than glycolic acid.

It loosens connections between dead skin cells and also acts as a humectant that supports hydration. Its larger molecule limits how deeply it penetrates. It has been studied for hyperpigmentation, including a trial of an 82 percent preparation in melasma, and salts such as ammonium lactate are common in moisturizers for dry skin.
quick.how: People use it in leave-on serums or lotions a few times a week, as occasional professional peels, or in body creams for rough skin, with sunscreen during the day. Smoother, softer skin tends to appear over several weeks.
quick.risks: Irritation, stinging and increased sun sensitivity occur, and professional-strength peels carry a risk of pigment changes. Sunscreen is advised. The name is shared with unrelated things such as lactic acid bacteria, injectable poly-L-lactic acid and muscle lactate.

angle.text: Lactic acid is used as a milder exfoliating acid for rough texture, dullness, uneven tone and dry body skin. It loosens dead skin and holds water, leaving skin softer and brighter. Controlled studies of its appearance effects are fewer than for glycolic acid.

ceramides.summary: Barrier lipids in moisturizers that lock in moisture and calm dry, flaky, irritated skin.

quick.overview:
Ceramides are waxy lipids that make up roughly half of the lipid matrix of the outer skin layer. Ceramide moisturizers, often with cholesterol and fatty acids, are used to repair a damaged barrier, ease dryness and flaking, and calm skin irritated by retinoids or exfoliating acids.

Topical ceramides replenish the lipid layers between skin cells, which reduces water loss and strengthens the barrier against irritants. Clinical trials generally show improved barrier function and hydration, and a 2025 review describes ceramide as a thoroughly studied compound used medically for barrier defects in atopic dermatitis and dry skin.
quick.how: People apply ceramide creams or lotions once or twice daily, often after cleansing and over or under actives like retinoids and acids to reduce irritation. Improvements in dryness and comfort are usually noticed within days to weeks. Results depend on the whole formula.
quick.risks: Ceramides are among the best-tolerated skincare ingredients, with rare allergic reactions usually traced to other ingredients in the product. They are sold over the counter. Anti-aging benefits are mostly indirect, through better hydration and barrier.

angle.text: Ceramide moisturizers are used to rebuild a damaged skin barrier, especially alongside retinoids and exfoliating acids. Skin holds more moisture, so dryness and flaking ease and skin looks calmer. Dermatology studies support their role in dry and eczema-prone skin.

urea.summary: Humectant and gentle exfoliant that smooths rough, dry, flaky or bumpy skin on body and feet.

quick.overview:
Urea is a natural part of the skin's moisturizing factor and is used in creams to smooth rough, dry, scaly or bumpy skin, including dry body skin, keratosis pilaris texture and calloused heels.

It attracts and binds water as a humectant, and at higher concentrations it breaks down hydrogen bonds in keratin so thick scale loosens and sheds. A 2021 review describes its emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, barrier-enhancing and antimicrobial properties, and it has a long record in dermatology.
quick.how: People apply urea creams or lotions to the body, elbows, knees and feet once or twice daily, with lower strengths for general dryness and higher strengths for thick, scaly areas. Softer skin is often noticeable within days to a couple of weeks. Facial use is less common.
quick.risks: Mild stinging is the main side effect, especially on cracked or inflamed skin and at higher strengths. It is available without a prescription in most markets. Facial anti-aging use has been little studied.

angle.text: Urea creams are used for rough, dry or bumpy skin on the body and feet, and sometimes for keratosis pilaris texture. Urea draws in and holds water and loosens dead scale, so skin feels and looks smoother. Its moisturizing and keratolytic role is well established in dermatology.

hyaluronic-acid.summary: Water-binding molecule for plump, hydrated skin; injectable forms are fillers that add volume to lips, cheeks and folds.

quick.overview:
Hyaluronic acid is a sugar-based molecule found in skin and joints that binds large amounts of water. In serums it gives temporary surface hydration and a plumper look; in cross-linked injectable gels it is used as a dermal filler to add volume to lips, cheeks, under-eyes and folds.

Topical products hydrate the outer skin layer, which smooths the look of fine lines for a time. Fillers physically add volume, with an effect that Wikipedia says lasts around 6 to 12 months, and they have US FDA regulatory approval. A 2022 review examined topical HA for skin quality and aging, and small trials have tested oral HA supplements.
quick.how: Serums are applied to damp skin once or twice daily and layered under moisturizer, often alongside other actives. Fillers are administered in a clinic by trained injectors, with results visible right away and refreshed periodically as they gradually dissolve.
quick.risks: Topical forms are very well tolerated. Fillers commonly cause short-lived bruising, swelling and lumps at the injection site. Rare severe complications include vascular occlusion leading to tissue damage or vision loss, and outcomes are associated with injector skill.

angle.text: Hyaluronic acid serums give temporary hydration and plumping, while injectable fillers reshape lips, cheeks and the under-eye area. It binds water, so skin looks fuller and fine lines look softer. Topical use gives short-lived hydration in studies, and fillers have extensive clinical use for volume.

ghk-cu.summary: Copper peptide used in creams, and in peptide blends, for skin texture, fine lines, acne scars and hair density.

quick.overview:
GHK-Cu is a naturally occurring copper-binding tripeptide found in plasma, saliva and urine, with levels reported to fall with age. It appears in anti-aging, firming and hair-care products as copper tripeptide-1, and people use it hoping for smoother skin, fewer fine lines, less visible acne scarring and thicker-looking hair.

It is proposed to act as a signalling molecule that stimulates collagen and glycosaminoglycan production and influences genes tied to tissue remodeling and inflammation. These mechanisms are mostly shown in cells and animals. Human appearance data are mainly small, short topical studies of anti-wrinkle and firming effects.
quick.how: Most people use it in topical serums and creams, often alongside other actives, with changes judged over weeks to months. Some users also take it in injectable peptide blends discussed on forums, which are sold as unapproved research products.
quick.risks: Topical use is usually well tolerated apart from occasional irritation. Injectable and compounded versions are not approved; the FDA states that compounded injectable drugs containing GHK-Cu may pose a risk of immunogenicity, with limited human data, and research-use peptides sold online vary in quality and purity.

angle.text: Users apply GHK-Cu, and some use it in peptide blends, to improve skin texture, fine lines, acne scars and hair density. The copper peptide signals collagen and tissue repair, so skin can look firmer and smoother. Human studies are mostly small topical cosmetic trials.

matrixyl.summary: Cosmetic peptide in serums and eye creams that signals collagen production to soften fine lines.

quick.overview:
Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4) is a cosmetic peptide used in serums, creams and eye products to soften wrinkles and fine lines, including around the eyes. It was launched in 2000 by the French ingredient maker Sederma.

The peptide is a fragment related to collagen breakdown that acts as a messenger, and in cell studies it stimulates production of type I and III collagen and other matrix components. A palmitic acid chain is attached to help it cross the skin's lipid barrier. Studies by the supplier and by independent groups have been published, and many human studies are small or compare it with other peptides.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily serum or cream, often combined with other peptides, retinoids and moisturizers, and judged over weeks to months. Results depend on the formulation and how much reaches the target skin layer.
quick.risks: It is considered low-risk, with rare irritation, and is freely sold as a cosmetic. Reported effects are modest.

angle.text: Matrixyl is a cosmetic peptide used in serums and creams to soften wrinkles and fine lines, including around the eyes. It signals skin cells to make collagen, so skin can look slightly firmer. Small studies, many manufacturer-linked, have measured modest wrinkle changes.

argireline.summary: Needle-free peptide marketed as topical Botox to relax the look of forehead lines and crow's feet.

quick.overview:
Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-8) is a short synthetic peptide applied to soften the look of expression lines, especially on the forehead and around the eyes. It is often marketed as a needle-free or botox-like alternative.

It is modelled on part of SNAP-25, a protein that botulinum toxin type A also targets, and is proposed to compete with it in the SNARE complex, slightly reducing neurotransmitter release and muscle contraction. Published human studies are small and short, some reporting reduced measured wrinkle depth over about four weeks. A 2025 review notes its passage through the skin barrier is limited and that no study has compared it directly with botulinum toxin.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or eye cream once or twice daily, often as part of a multi-ingredient anti-aging routine, and judged over several weeks. Effects reported are far milder than injected toxin.
quick.risks: It is generally well tolerated and sold as a cosmetic. Skin penetration is reported to be limited, so real-world results vary.

angle.text: Users apply Argireline as a needle-free alternative to Botox for forehead lines and crow's feet. The peptide imitates part of a protein botulinum toxin targets, to slightly dampen the muscle signal behind expression lines. Studies are small and short, and how much reaches the muscle is debated.

snap-8.summary: Argireline-family peptide in serums and eye creams that softens forehead and eye-area expression lines.

quick.overview:
SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-3) is a longer relative of Argireline used in serums and eye creams to soften expression lines on the forehead and around the eyes. It is often described as a stronger version of Argireline.

It is built on the same SNAP-25-derived sequence and is proposed to interfere with SNARE complex assembly, reducing neurotransmitter release at the muscle junction in a way conceptually similar to botulinum toxin but milder and reversible. A 2020 review reported no peer-reviewed clinical study of the peptide on its own and noted that the wrinkle-reduction figures in circulation come from the manufacturer.
quick.how: It is applied as a daily serum or eye cream, usually as one ingredient among several in anti-aging products, with changes judged over weeks. Injectable versions are discussed only on forums.
quick.risks: It is considered low risk and is unrestricted as a cosmetic ingredient. Reported effects are modest and reversible, and skin delivery is reported to limit its effect.

angle.text: SNAP-8 is used in serums and eye creams to soften forehead and eye-area expression lines, and is described as a longer relative of Argireline. It imitates part of a muscle-signalling protein to reduce contraction slightly. Claims come mainly from manufacturer data, and independent human trials are scarce.

carnosine.summary: Antioxidant, anti-glycation dipeptide taken or applied to slow collagen damage and skin aging.

quick.overview:
Carnosine is a dipeptide of beta-alanine and histidine found at high levels in muscle and brain. It is sold as an oral supplement and added to some skincare, where it is used by people aiming to slow skin aging.

The idea is that it limits glycation, the sugar-driven cross-linking of proteins such as collagen, and scavenges reactive oxygen species and metal ions, so skin ages more slowly. Laboratory work shows these effects, while evidence for visible skin improvement in people is limited. Its best human evidence concerns beta-alanine supplementation, which raises muscle carnosine and has been studied for exercise performance.
quick.how: People take it as a capsule or powder, or use it in serums and creams, and some include it in supplement stacks with other antioxidants. Any skin effects would be expected to build over months.
quick.risks: It is generally well tolerated. Beta-alanine supplementation can cause tingling. Carnosine is found in meat but not in plant foods.

angle.text: Carnosine is taken orally or applied in skincare by users who want to slow skin aging. It acts as an antioxidant and limits sugar cross-linking of collagen, so skin may age more slowly. Most data are from lab and animal studies, with limited human skin results.

spironolactone.summary: Prescription antiandrogen that reduces oil and clears hormonal acne, also used for hair and body-hair concerns.

quick.overview:
Spironolactone is a prescription diuretic that also blocks androgen receptors. Dermatologists prescribe it off-label for persistent hormonal acne in adult women, and it is also used for hirsutism and female pattern hair loss. Appearance-focused users also discuss it for water retention and DHT-related hair loss.

By blocking androgen signalling it reduces sebum output, so there is less oil to clog pores and fewer breakouts. The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes a conditional recommendation for it, and two randomised trials, SAFA in England and Wales and FASCE in France, tested it in adult women with acne.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily tablet under medical supervision, often alongside topical acne treatments, with a prescriber monitoring blood potassium. Improvement in acne generally develops over a few months. Use in men for acne is rare, and hair and puffiness use is largely off-label.
quick.risks: Side effects include menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, dizziness and raised potassium. Prescribing information warns of hyperkalaemia and gynecomastia and reports feminisation of male fetuses in rat studies, so it is not used in pregnancy, and its feminizing effects limit use in men. It requires a prescription and monitoring.

angle.text: Spironolactone is a prescription antiandrogen and diuretic used for hormonal acne, and discussed for DHT-related hair loss, body hair and water retention. It blocks androgen receptors, so skin makes less oil and breaks out less. Acne use in women is clinically studied; male and hair use is largely off-label, with feminizing side effects.

clascoterone.summary: Topical antiandrogen cream approved for acne, clearing breakouts without systemic hormone effects; studied for hair loss.

quick.overview:
Clascoterone (Winlevi) is a 1 percent topical antiandrogen cream approved by the FDA in August 2020 for acne in patients aged 12 and older, and considered a first-in-class medicine. People use it for clearer skin without taking a hormone-blocking pill. A higher-strength solution has been tested for androgenetic alopecia, which interests hairline-focused users.

It competes with dihydrotestosterone for androgen receptors in oil glands and hair follicles, so there is less oil and inflammation locally. In two phase 3 trials of about 1,440 participants, roughly 18 to 21 percent of clascoterone users reached treatment success at 12 weeks versus about 7 to 9 percent on vehicle.
quick.how: It is applied as a prescription cream to affected acne areas twice daily over a course of months, often alongside other acne treatments, and judged over about 12 weeks. Hair-loss use is investigational and not approved.
quick.risks: Local redness, dryness and itching are the most common effects. The label warns about reversible suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and raised potassium in some trial participants. The European Medicines Agency initially recommended refusal in April 2025, then granted authorisation in October 2025 after re-examination. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Clascoterone is a topical antiandrogen cream used on the skin for acne without systemic hormone effects. It blocks androgen receptors in the skin, so there is less oil and inflammation and skin clears. Acne use is approved and trial-backed; for hair loss it is still under study.

pdrn-polynucleotides.summary: DNA-fragment skin boosters, injected or topical, used for skin quality, scars and post-procedure recovery.

quick.overview:
PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide) is a mixture of DNA fragments, typically purified from salmon or trout sperm, used in injectable and topical skin booster treatments for rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after lasers or microneedling. It is widely used in Asian aesthetic clinics.

PDRN is proposed to act through adenosine receptor activation and by supplying nucleotides, supporting fibroblast activity, new blood vessels and calmer inflammation so skin repairs and texture improves. Polynucleotides (PN) are made of longer DNA chains and are described as acting mainly on matrix remodelling. The best-established clinical evidence concerns wound healing such as diabetic foot ulcers; a 2025 systematic review of polynucleotides in aesthetic medicine found nine studies covering 219 patients.
quick.how: It is usually given as a series of clinic treatments by small injections or applied topically after procedures, with products varying in source, molecule size and technique. Skin quality changes are typically judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Injection can cause bruising, infection and allergy, particularly to fish-derived material. Regulatory status varies, and many cosmetic products are not approved as drugs. Results differ by product.

angle.text: PDRN and polynucleotide skin boosters are injected or applied for skin rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after lasers or microneedling. DNA fragments support tissue repair, so skin quality and texture improve. Clinical studies exist for wound healing; cosmetic studies are smaller and vary by product.

omega-3-epa-dha.summary: Fish-oil fats taken for calmer, less inflamed skin, recovery and general health.

quick.overview:
Omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA come from oily fish, fish oil and algae. In appearance circles they are a baseline supplement taken for calmer skin, less redness and dryness, and better recovery, and some users hope for less puffiness and better hair.

EPA and DHA are built into cell membranes and serve as precursors to resolvins and protectins, which help end inflammation, so inflamed skin can settle. Trials of EPA and DHA for skin outcomes are few and mixed. The best-established regulatory use of purified EPA and DHA is lowering triglycerides in severe hypertriglyceridemia.
quick.how: People take them as fish-oil, krill-oil or algal-oil capsules or liquids daily with meals, or get them from oily fish, as part of a general health and recovery stack. Any skin changes would be expected to build over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Fish oil can cause fishy aftertaste and digestive upset, and high doses may raise bleeding risk or affect heart rhythm in some people. Contaminant and oxidation quality vary by product. Supplements are sold over the counter.

angle.text: Users take fish oil for its anti-inflammatory fats, hoping for calmer, clearer skin, less puffiness, better hair and better recovery. EPA and DHA help switch off inflammation, so skin can look less red and irritated. Trials exist for inflammation and some skin conditions; direct appearance effects are less studied.

zinc.summary: Essential mineral that calms inflammatory acne and corrects deficiency-related hair shedding.

quick.overview:
Zinc is an essential mineral taken as an oral supplement and used in topical products such as zinc oxide sunscreens and acne formulations. People use it for inflammatory acne, redness and hair shedding linked to deficiency.

It supports enzyme function, wound healing, immune regulation and skin-cell biology and has mild anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects. A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis found people with acne had lower serum zinc than controls and that zinc treatment, alone or as an adjunct, was associated with significant improvement in inflammatory papule counts, without a significant difference in side effects versus comparators. Benefits are clearest when a deficiency is corrected.
quick.how: People take it as a daily supplement, often with meals, or use it topically in creams and sunscreens, usually alongside other acne or hair routines. Some pair it with copper because of mineral balance. Skin changes are typically judged over weeks to months.
quick.risks: High-dose supplementation can cause nausea and, over time, copper deficiency, and excess intake may cause ataxia and lethargy. Intake above requirements has not been shown to add benefit. Zinc is available without prescription.

angle.text: Users take or apply zinc for inflammatory acne, redness and hair shedding tied to deficiency. The mineral supports skin and immune function, so inflammation and shedding ease and skin and hair look healthier. Evidence exists for acne and deficiency-related hair loss; hormone, voice and height claims are anecdotal.
